problemStatement:
Problem Addressed: Common heatsinks provide a fixed level of cooling regardless of the thermal load. A large heatsink can provide better cooling but is generally heavier, more expensive, and occupies more space. A small heatsink is more compact but may be incapable of handling a sudden temperature spike. THERMOR-R addresses this problem by providing an adjustable cooling surface according to the thermal load.
Hardware Solution: THERMOR-R makes use of a central fixed aluminium heatsink with deployable side-fin panels on hinges. Three 10 W power resistors provide controlled heating via an aluminium spreader. A FAST bimetal strip reacts quickly to a temperature increase, whereas a SLOW bimetal strip with additional thermal mass reacts more slowly to a temperature increase. The difference in movement caused by the two bimetals is used to operate a lever, release a latch, and deploy the side fins by means of a spring. A separate critical-temperature thermostat provides an alternative means of operating the mechanism, and a return spring allows the mechanism to be reset once the temperature has decreased. Thermocouples, MAX6675 modules, an ESP32, and an OLED display are used to monitor temperatures and operating mode.
Innovation: The main innovation of this project is the use of the thermal response of bimetals to mechanically deploy additional cooling surface area, as opposed to a more conventional sensor–microcontroller–motor setup. The difference between the response of the FAST and the SLOW bimetal is effectively used as an indicator of a rapidly increasing temperature, which causes additional cooling surface to be deployed automatically. A separate thermostat is used to provide protection against dangerously high temperatures. The transparent prototype will also serve to demonstrate and experiment with the concept, and allow the mechanism to be compared directly with a conventional heatsink.

workingPrinciple:
THERMOR-R makes use of a passive thermal to mechanical control sequence, where the application of heat itself triggers the cooling system. This commences by the provision of three 10 W power resistors, that apply controlled heat to the heatsink via an aluminium spreader.
At higher temperatures two bimetal thermal elements act at differing rates, the first being FAST and the second SLOW (having additional thermal mass). The differing actuation rates are apparent at slow heating, where the two actuators move together with only a small difference in distance travelled. However, during a faster temperature rise, the faster responding FAST bimetal moves further than the slower SLOW bimetal, causing a noticeable displacement in a mechanical lever.
This provides mechanical advantage and unlatches deployable side fins from a holding latch, allowing a loaded spring to swing hinged aluminium side-fin panels outwards, enhancing the surface area available for passive heat dissipation.
A separate critical-temperature thermostat provides backup in the event of an extreme temperature rise (without sufficient FAST-SLOW actuation difference to trigger the deployment mechanism). As temperatures decrease, the thermal elements relax towards their original position, and a return spring acts to reset the side-fin panels towards the closed position. This provides three possible operating modes-NORMAL, BOOST and MAXIMUM COOLING.
For monitoring and displaying purposes, K-type thermocouples, MAX6675 modules, an ESP32 and an OLED display are used to measure temperatures and indicate the operating mode.
potentialImpact:
THERMOR-R would be useful in any industry which is concerned with cooling down power electronics, LED's, charging systems and possibly transportation electronics. It's simplest in it's ability to provide extra cooling when needed. 
Rather than having a heatsink of a fixed size that is always present and removing heat at a fixed rate, THERMOR-R could allow for a smaller footprint while still allowing extra cooling when temperatures rise. This could be acheived by adding mechanically deployed heat dissipating elements rather than having them always deployed. This would be useful in applications where mechanical simplicity, low power requirements, and passive cooling are desired. Rather than being controlled by electronics to deploy or change, the surface area would be changed by being mechanically pushed out by thermal expansion rather than electronic means. 
The benefit to the end user or manufacturer is potentially much greater cooling performance in a mechanically simpler device than a fixed passive heatsink. The system would need to be tested against conventional heatsinks in order to be able to claim lower temperatures, quicker cooling, reduced costs, or increased reliability.
auraDemoHighlight:
The most impressive part about THERMOR-R is that the heat itself transforms the heatsink physically in order to increase its cooling capacity, mechanically, without the need for anything else.
Typical heatsinks have a static cooling surface, but THERMOR-R takes an entirely different approach in which it is typically compact, but features two bimetal elements which move differently when subjected to rapid increases in temperature, mechanically pushing a lever and releasing a latch, allowing the spring-loaded aluminium fins to automatically deploy, increasing the surface area of the heatsink and thus its cooling capacity.
What makes the project especially interesting is that the main procedure is completely passive and mechanical, the electronics only serving the purpose of measuring and validating the temperature. This means that the project offers a physical and mechanical experience of a system which transforms itself in reaction to the temperature, in real time.
The project acts as a demonstration of thermal expansion, mechanical leverage and energy stored in springs being employed in a single, fully functional mechanism. Rather than a display of electronics, it serves more as a display of mechanical engineering and a clever application of bimetallic mechanics.
